text:
A rate rise reprices every house without touching a single brick. Between March 2022 and July 2023, the Federal Reserve raised its policy rate from near zero to 5.25–5.5%. Over that period, the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate climbed from roughly 3% to above 7%. That rate follows ten-year Treasury yields more closely than it follows Fed announcements.

On a $400,000 loan, the monthly payment rose from about $1,686 to $2,661. Buyers found that they could borrow more than a third less than before, and old prices no longer passed the affordability math.

Owners with loans under 4% also stayed where they were, because moving would mean giving up their cheap loans. Few homes came up for sale as a result. Sales dropped before prices did: US existing-home sales fell to 4.09 million in 2023, the lowest since 1995.

Credit is what keeps the housing market going. Higher rates make it scarcer, and demand weakens.
